description:
## Goal

Make protocol-domain obligations enforceable at user callsites.

For `@spec use(Enumerable.t(integer)) :: integer`:

- `[1]` is accepted when `Enumerable` has a `List` implementation.
- `[:bad]` is rejected because its element does not satisfy `integer`.
- `1` is rejected when `Enumerable` has no `Integer` implementation.

Keep `Protocol.t(...)` as a declaration-owned marker. Do not turn its
`TypeDefined` fact into a union of currently known implementations or couple
runtime dispatch to the marker type.

## Current behavior at main a3a9761d1

`resolve.rs` resolves an opaque declaration's body but constructs the hard type
as only `opaque_of(tag)`. `TypeDef.params` retains the formal ids, but the marker
body contains no occurrence of them, so applying `t(integer)` and `t(atom)`
produces the same hard marker.

`ResolvedContractArrow` correctly classifies that marker into a
`ProtocolDomainObligation`. However, `FunctionContract::apply` defines an arrow
as structurally enforceable only when its obligation set is empty. A contract
containing only a protocol-domain arrow therefore cannot emit a fatal
`spec/violation`.

The current obligation key contains the protocol marker tag, but does not retain
enough application evidence to validate the receiver's implementation and bind
`t(a)`'s `a`.

This is distinct from protocol callback dispatch. `resolve_protocol_call`
already selects implementations directly from receiver/implementation-target
overlap; protocol `TypeDefined` facts and protocol dispatch facts intentionally
have separate ownership.

## Repro

```fz
defprotocol Enumerable do
  fn reduce(enumerable, acc, reducer)
end

defimpl Enumerable, for: List do
  fn reduce(list, acc, reducer), do: acc
end

defmodule M do
  @spec use(Enumerable.t(integer)) :: integer
  fn use(_xs), do: 1
end

fn main() do
  dbg(M.use([1]))
  dbg(M.use([:bad]))
  dbg(M.use(1))
end
```

At a3a9761d1:

```text
$ fz2 run --dump activations=activations.txt repro.fz
1
1
1
exit=0

M.use/1[[:bad]]
M.use/1[[int]]
M.use/1[int]
```

Both invalid calls reach activations instead of producing `spec/violation`.

## Required work

- Preserve enough resolved protocol-application evidence on each contract
  obligation to identify the protocol, affected parameter position, type
  arguments, and shared variables/bounds.
- Derive protocol-domain validation from protocol-owned facts. Contract
  application must not rewalk source syntax or redefine the protocol marker as
  an implementation union.
- For a ground observed receiver, decide whether an applicable implementation
  exists. Pending relevant protocol facts must wait rather than falsely reject.
- When the obligation is `Protocol.t(a)`, bind `a` from the matched receiver
  domain and use that binding in the remaining parameters and result.
- Include a protocol-domain arrow in satisfaction, refinement, and fatal
  enforcement only after its obligations are validated.
- Remove the blanket `obligations.is_empty()` enforcement exemption once every
  obligation has a decidable validation result.
- Preserve the existing separation between marker `TypeDefined` facts and
  implementation-target runtime dispatch.

## Checks

- The existing marker ownership test remains green: `t/0` and `t/1` retain the
  declaration-owned marker and loading an impl revises dispatch, not the marker.
- `Enumerable.t(integer)` accepts `[1]` when the List impl exists.
- `Enumerable.t(integer)` rejects `[:bad]` with `spec/violation`.
- `Enumerable.t(integer)` rejects `1` with `spec/violation` when no Integer impl
  exists.
- A dependent contract such as
  `@spec pick(Enumerable.t(a), a) :: a` accepts `pick([1], 2)` and rejects
  `pick([1], :bad)`, proving that `a` is bound from the receiver.
- No accepted protocol-domain call relies on `refine_contract_inputs` returning
  the observed input after an empty intersection.
- Mixed protocol/concrete overload enforcement remains green, including
  `spec_mixed_protocol_concrete_violation`.
- Full library and fixture matrix pass with no protocol dispatch regressions.
title: Protocol-domain @spec obligations are never validated, so non-implementers and wrong t(a) elements are accepted
